target: AG1's claim that a federal/national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers for voters
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or give paid time off, so many private-sector hourly workers—especially in retail and service jobs—would still have to work and would not automatically get the time off needed to vote.

target: AG1's claim that a national holiday would reduce scheduling barriers for millions of Americans
objection: Low-income workers are disproportionately concentrated in hourly retail and service jobs and are less able to absorb unpaid time off, so they are especially likely to keep working or lose wages even if Election Day is a federal holiday.

target: AG2's claim that a national holiday would still leave a similarly large share of voters unable to take sufficient time to vote because private employers need not close
objection: In practice many private-sector employers observe federal holidays by giving paid holiday time or reducing operating hours, so many hourly workers would actually gain time off or schedule flexibility on Election Day.

target: AG2's claim that many private-sector workers would still be unable to vote on a holiday
objection: Private-sector workers make up a substantial share of voters, and if many of them get holiday flexibility, it is no longer supported to say a holiday would still leave a similarly large share unable to take sufficient time to vote.

target: AG2's claim that holiday scheduling would typically leave a similarly large share of voters unable to take sufficient time to vote, based on private-sector work constraints
objection: The fact that many OECD democracies hold elections on weekends or holidays suggests this scheduling is workable even with large private sectors, so holiday election timing does not usually leave an overwhelmingly large share of voters unable to vote.

target: AG2's assumption that only private-sector work matters to time barriers on Election Day
objection: School obligations are also a major part of the barrier to voting, and a national holiday would give many people, including students and caregivers tied to school schedules, more available time to vote.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday would still leave a similarly large share of voters unable to take sufficient time to vote
objection: If school-day constraints are reduced for many voters, then it is not well-supported to say that a holiday would still leave a similarly large share unable to vote, even if some private-sector workers still have to work.

target: AG2's assumption that the main voting-time burden is just having a paid day off rather than the total time cost of voting
objection: Travel and waiting time are also part of the burden, and a holiday would likely increase poll-worker availability and election staffing, which would shorten lines and reduce the total time needed to vote.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday would still leave a large share of voters unable to take sufficient time to vote
objection: If waiting times fall, even workers who still have shifts can fit voting into shorter windows before or after work, so the conclusion that a large share would still be blocked is not warranted.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday would still leave a similarly large share of voters unable to vote because of time barriers
objection: Child-care and supervision conflicts are another major part of the time barrier to voting, and a national holiday would reduce those conflicts for many parents and guardians.

target: AG2's claim that persistent work barriers mean a holiday would still leave a similarly large share of voters unable to vote
objection: If child-care and supervision conflicts are reduced, then a major source of 'not enough time' to vote is alleviated, including for people who still must work at employers that remain open.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday would still leave a similarly large share of voters unable to vote because of time barriers
objection: A national holiday would likely reduce commute and travel congestion, which lowers the time cost of getting to polling places and makes in-person voting more manageable.

target: AG2's assumption that a holiday's effect is limited to work/school calendars
objection: Even workers who cannot take a full day off may be able to vote in smaller windows if a holiday reduces travel and waiting time, so the holiday can lower the practical voting burden more broadly.

target: AG2's claim that workers would still need a fully paid day off to vote
objection: Making voting a celebrated civic occasion can encourage employers and community institutions to accommodate voting with schedule flexibility, so workers would not depend only on receiving a fully paid day off.

target: AG2's assumption that holiday recognition would be only symbolic and not affect behavior
objection: A national holiday's civic meaning can lead to practical accommodations, such as easier permission to step out and vote, which would reduce time barriers.

target: AG2's claim that workers still need a full uninterrupted day off to vote
objection: In-person voting takes only a limited amount of time, and on a holiday workplaces often have more flexible staffing, allowing many workers to use short windows before, after, or during shifts.

target: AG2's assumption that workplaces would remain too rigid on a holiday for workers to find time to vote
objection: A national holiday can reduce practical time barriers even when businesses stay open, because staffing and scheduling are often more flexible on holidays.

target: AG1's claim that research and turnout logic support a national holiday as a voting-access reform
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase turnout, especially compared with other reforms such as automatic voter registration or state-mandated time off to vote.

target: AG1's implication that a national holiday is the best or primary reform for voting access
objection: More reliable approaches exist—state laws requiring employer time off for voting and automatic voter registration—so a holiday is not the strongest policy choice.

target: AG2's claim that a national holiday disadvantages low-income workers
objection: Reducing scheduling barriers helps people with the least flexibility the most, so a national holiday would help low-income workers vote rather than disadvantage them.

target: AG2's claim that a national holiday should be rejected because it disadvantages low-income workers and is not reliably effective on its own
objection: If a policy reduces barriers for millions of voters, especially low-income workers, and also increases practical participation and civic importance, then it is justified rather than rejected.

target: AG2's claim that a national holiday would not meaningfully reduce the barriers that stop many people from voting
objection: The main problem on Election Day is that school and work schedules block many people, and a national holiday would directly reduce those scheduling barriers and make voting more feasible.

target: AG2's claim that a national holiday is disadvantageous to low-income workers
objection: Low-income workers are the people most constrained by rigid schedules and unpaid time off, so reducing schedule constraints would help them rather than hurt them.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is not justified as a national reform because it does not meaningfully reduce key barriers
objection: Removing major schedule barriers and increasing feasible participation, combined with broad public support and international precedent, is enough to justify making Election Day a national holiday.

target: AG1's claim that reducing Election Day scheduling barriers is enough to reliably increase turnout
objection: A national holiday mainly affects calendars; it does not change registration rules, ballot-access rules, or early/absentee voting options, and turnout is also constrained by those other barriers.

target: AG1's assumption that reducing scheduling barriers alone is sufficient to increase turnout
objection: Because voter participation is limited by multiple kinds of barriers, cutting Election Day scheduling barriers by itself is not enough to reliably boost turnout across the electorate.

target: AG1's claim that a national holiday would proportionally help low-income voters
objection: Low-income voters face higher time and money costs overall, so even if a holiday reduces some scheduling conflicts, it will not proportionally remove the broader obstacles they face.

target: AG1's assumption that a federal holiday would automatically reduce the practical time needed to vote
objection: The time burden of in-person voting includes travel and especially waiting in line, and simply having a holiday does not automatically reduce those parts of the process.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday will reliably improve voting access by itself
objection: A holiday can increase the number of people trying to vote without increasing polling-place capacity, which can produce longer waits that offset any scheduling benefit.

target: AG1's assumption that a national holiday would reliably remove school-day supervision and childcare barriers
objection: A federal holiday does not force most schools to close, since school calendars are local, so parents and guardians may still face childcare and supervision obligations on Election Day.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday would especially help low-income voters by reducing schedule barriers
objection: Low-income families typically have fewer affordable childcare alternatives and less flexibility to rearrange caregiving, so persistent supervision conflicts would continue to burden them.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday would reliably give private workers time to vote
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid leave, so many private-sector hourly workers would still have to work or lose wages to vote.

target: AG1's claim that a national holiday would help low-income workers rather than disadvantage them
objection: Because low-income workers are overrepresented in private-sector hourly jobs, a holiday that does not guarantee paid time off is likely to leave them working or losing wages, which disadvantages them.

target: AG1's claim that a national holiday is justified because it reduces schedule barriers and raises participation
objection: If research shows an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy and better reforms are available, then a holiday is not justified as the primary national reform.
